clue.text: Publication several hours behind ours

parts.note: a newspaper named after an American city whose clock runs about five hours behind British time, so its 'times' lag ours

explanation.surface: A periodical that always comes out late compared with ours.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a slow publication; the joke is that the city's clock time, not its printing, is hours behind London's.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous Manhattan daily paper takes its title from a city in the Eastern time zone, five hours behind Britain.

clue.text: Lunatic cuts no ice, endlessly wandering

indicators.note: the lunatic's word cuts into the other letters, sitting inside them

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: ice loses its final letter, so it has no end

parts.note: the frozen water word, here trimmed
a lunatic is mad

explanation.surface: A madman breaks through the ice, roaming aimlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' belongs with the ice, not the wandering, leaving IC; 'cuts' has the lunatic break into that frozen pair of pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomads roam from place to place without a fixed home, so the adjective describes a roving life.

clue.text: Old assembly I want reformed

indicators.note: formed again in a new shape, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wishes an ancient council were reorganised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reformed' rearranges I WANT. The Witan was the council of Anglo-Saxon kings.
explanation.definitionFit: The Witenagemot, or Witan, was the advisory council of Anglo-Saxon English kings.

clue.text: Go too far, having lofty aims?

explanation.surface: An ambitious person risks overreaching.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is cryptic: someone aiming high might shoot above the target.
explanation.definitionFit: To exceed a limit is to overreach; firing above a target is literally aiming too high, a playful reading of ambition.

clue.text: Out of luck. I will get the bird

indicators.note: the answer comes out of the run of words that follows, lying inside them

explanation.surface: An unlucky person resolves to win the girl after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of' looks like 'unlucky', but it signals that the letters lie inside 'luck. I will', ignoring the full stop.
explanation.definitionFit: A flightless bird native to New Zealand, also the country's emblem.

clue.text: Doolittle's suggestion to less refined burglar

indicators.note: Eliza Doolittle of Pygmalion speaks Cockney and drops her aitches, so the word loses its H

parts.note: a suggestion is a hint
more coarse, ruder

explanation.surface: Eliza Doolittle advises a coarse housebreaker.
explanation.walkthrough: Eliza Doolittle, Shaw's Cockney flower girl, drops her aitches, so HINT becomes 'INT; RUDER is joined 'to' it.
explanation.definitionFit: A burglar is an unwelcome intruder who breaks into a home.

clue.text: He devised changes, to the German code

definitions.text: He devised changes, to the German code

parts.words: He devised changes, to the German code
parts.note: a composer who wrote a set of variations ('changes') on a theme called Enigma, the name also of the German wartime cipher machine

explanation.surface: Someone altered a secret German cipher.
explanation.walkthrough: The wartime-cipher picture misleads: 'changes' are musical variations, and Enigma is the title of the work as well as the German code machine.
explanation.definitionFit: The English composer wrote the Enigma Variations, a set of musical variations on a hidden theme.

clue.text: Go to Luke for success in test

parts.note: to go, as in passing in a card game, is to pass
the Gospel that sits next to Luke's in the New Testament is Mark's

explanation.surface: Someone is told to consult Luke to do well in an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to Luke' means next to Luke: Mark's Gospel comes just before Luke's.
explanation.definitionFit: A pass mark is the minimum score that counts as a pass in an examination.

clue.text: Steady deterioration caused stoppage

indicators.note: the word falls apart, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Slow, steady decline brought things to a halt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deterioration' rearranges STEADY.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay something is to halt or check it, as a court stays an execution.

clue.text: Common sense lacked by, old man?

explanation.surface: Father is said to have no practical sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is cryptic: the wit belonging to a mother is what a father, the 'old man', does not have.
explanation.definitionFit: Native good sense is mother-wit; read literally it is mother's wit, which a father lacks.

clue.text: Convey the president

explanation.surface: Passing something on to the head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: Ulysses S. Grant was the 18th US president.
explanation.definitionFit: To grant is to bestow or transfer formally; Ulysses S. Grant was a US president.

clue.text: Article used in recipe for a sort of pastry

indicators.note: the article word is placed inside the other

parts.note: a dish is a prepared recipe
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Instructions for a pastry call for a particular item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used in' signals a container; 'recipe' stands loosely for the dish it produces.
explanation.definitionFit: A Danish is a sweet yeasted breakfast pastry, often with fruit or icing.

clue.text: Island off the Needles?

explanation.surface: An island lying off the Needles, the rocks off the Isle of Wight.
explanation.walkthrough: The Needles are chalk rocks off the Isle of Wight, but here they are knitting needles: the second sense is a knitted sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: A Channel Island, and a thick knitted woollen sweater that comes off knitting needles.

clue.text: Simpleton appearing regularly to make strike calls

definitions.text: appearing regularly to make strike calls

explanation.surface: A fool keeps turning up to announce walkouts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike calls' are not industrial action: a clock bird pops out on the hour as the clock strikes.
explanation.definitionFit: A silly person is called by the bird's name; the bird in a novelty clock appears every hour to sound the time.

clue.text: Cold type of cleaner required for Duke's carriage

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold on taps

indicators.note: a type of cleaner is a variant form of the word, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A duke needs a cold kind of cleaning product for his coach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'type of' rearranges the cleaner's letters, giving LARENCE after the cold tap's letter. The carriage was named after the Duke of Clarence, later William IV.
explanation.definitionFit: The closed four-wheeled horse-drawn coach was named after the Duke of Clarence, later William IV.

clue.text: Coast used by surfer

explanation.surface: A shoreline frequented by surfers.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is read as two words: a surfer uses a board on the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The land along the sea is the shore; split, the word names a surfer's board for the waves.

clue.text: Indian jet covers short distance

indicators.note: in a down clue the first word sits on top of the second, covering it

parts.note: jet black is a deep black
a foot is a short length

explanation.surface: A jet aircraft flies over a brief stretch of India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian' means a Native American, not someone from India; 'covers' puts BLACK above FOOT in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The Blackfoot are a Native American people of the northern Plains.

clue.text: This state comes to pass, or there's trouble

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass
taken as written
ado means fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: A situation arises, or else there's bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This state' is the US state, not a condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Colorado is a Rocky Mountain state of the USA.

clue.text: Part right behind leader in minority group

indicators.note: the letter goes just after the first letter of the group word, behind its leader

parts.note: a faction is a dissenting group within a larger body

explanation.surface: Part of the right supports the leader of a breakaway group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'behind leader in' puts R after the F of FACTION.
explanation.definitionFit: A fraction is a portion or piece of a whole.

clue.text: Crew's quarters reduced by 40% altogether

parts.note: the ten-letter word for the crew's quarters at a ship's bow is shortened by four letters in its contracted spelling

explanation.surface: Sailors' living space has been cut back substantially.
explanation.walkthrough: The full form, forecastle, has ten letters; its contracted spelling drops four, i.e. 40 per cent.
explanation.definitionFit: The forward part of a ship where sailors are housed is the forecastle, contracted in speech and writing.

clue.text: Carrier is astern of sailing vessel'

indicators.note: behind, in nautical terms, so IS comes after the ship word

parts.note: a bark or barque is a sailing ship
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cargo carrier is behind a sailing ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carrier' is not a ship: Barkis is the carrier (a carter) in Dickens's David Copperfield.
explanation.definitionFit: Barkis, the carter in Dickens's David Copperfield, is famous for saying he is willing.

clue.text: Constable's superior, it's said, as painter

indicators.note: spoken, so the word sounds like the one wanted

parts.note: a police sergeant ranks above a constable

explanation.surface: A homophone puts a police rank next to John Constable's art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constable' looks like the painter but is a police officer, outranked by a sergeant; John Singer Sargent was a portrait painter.
explanation.definitionFit: John Singer Sargent was an American portrait painter of the late 19th century.

clue.text: Performing with distinction, initially in Devon

indicators.note: the distinction word comes first, before the performing word

parts.note: a credit is an exam grade of distinction
on means on stage, performing

explanation.surface: An actor gives an excellent show in Devon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' puts the distinction first, ahead of the performing word. Crediton is a market town in Devon, a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Crediton is a small market town in mid-Devon, north-west of Exeter.

clue.text: Reference section we have on hand

explanation.surface: A library section is within reach.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is cryptic: everyone has an index finger on each hand.
explanation.definitionFit: The alphabetical list at the back of a book is for reference; the forefinger is on everyone's hand.

clue.text: Run through with more bias

explanation.surface: Stabbing someone with greater prejudice.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the word as a comparative: more skew.
explanation.definitionFit: To pierce with a spit is to impale; as a comparative, more slanted.

clue.text: Innocent naturalist

explanation.surface: A blameless student of nature.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert White wrote The Natural History of Selborne.
explanation.definitionFit: Pure and blameless is lily-white; Gilbert White was an English naturalist.

clue.text: Fish is distressed, caught in it

indicators.note: the caught letter goes in it, the distressed word just named

parts.note: to be distressed is to be sad
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A fish is upset at being trapped in something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in it' puts C inside SAD.
explanation.definitionFit: The scad is a horse mackerel, a sea fish.

clue.text: Dashed with spirit, unlike Wellington?

explanation.surface: A spirited dash, unlike the Iron Duke.
explanation.walkthrough: Wellington is not the Duke but the rubber boot, which is pulled on rather than tied with laces.
explanation.definitionFit: A drink with a dash of liquor is spiked; shoes fastened with strings are tied, unlike pull-on rubber boots.

clue.text: Recluse, note, a rich eccentric

indicators.note: odd and off-centre, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A hermit turns out to be an eccentric wealthy man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' rearranges NOTE A RICH.
explanation.definitionFit: An anchorite is a religious hermit who withdraws from society.

clue.text: Capital way to get to Exeter or Lincoln

definitions.text: to get to Exeter or Lincoln

explanation.surface: Directions to two English cities via a London street.
explanation.walkthrough: Exeter and Lincoln are not the cities but Oxford colleges; the street is London's shopping thoroughfare.
explanation.definitionFit: A major London shopping street; and literally a street to Oxford, home of Exeter and Lincoln colleges.
